headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Polycythaemia
headings.content: Polycythaemia is a haematological disorder characterized by an abnormal increase in the volume of circulating red blood cells, leading to an elevated packed cell volume, haemoglobin concentration, and total red cell mass. In clinical practice, this is frequently identified when the haematocrit levels significantly exceed normal physiological ranges for age and sex. This excess production of erythrocytes increases whole blood viscosity, which subsequently impedes microvascular blood flow and impairs tissue perfusion across vital organs. Nursing students must understand that polycythaemia is not merely an isolated lab value abnormality, but a systemic condition that can severely compromise cardiovascular and cerebrovascular health if left unrecognized or unmanaged. The condition can present acutely or insidiously, requiring thorough patient assessments to detect subtle changes in oxygenation, perfusion, and neurological status early in the disease process. Recognizing these foundational definitions allows nurses to anticipate the physiological strain placed on the heart and vascular networks, forming the basis for safe and effective clinical interventions within Nigerian healthcare settings where chronic hypoxaemia from endemic pulmonary conditions or high-altitude living may also play contributing roles. Comprehending this baseline pathology ensures that nursing care plans prioritize hydration, circulation monitoring, and patient education regarding lifestyle modifications to mitigate thrombotic risks.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Mechanisms
headings.content: The pathophysiology of polycythaemia is fundamentally rooted in the dysregulation of erythropoiesis, the process by which red blood cells are produced in the bone marrow. Normally, erythropoiesis is tightly regulated by the hormone erythropoietin (EPO), which is synthesized primarily by the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidneys in response to tissue hypoxia. When systemic oxygen levels drop, renal sensors stimulate EPO secretion, signaling bone marrow stem cells to accelerate erythroid progenitor proliferation. In polycythaemia, this feedback loop is disrupted. In primary forms, the bone marrow pluripotent stem cells undergo clonal mutations, such as the JAK2V617F mutation, allowing them to produce red blood cells independently of normal EPO control. Consequently, serum EPO levels are characteristically low or undetectable because the autonomous marrow expansion suppresses normal renal hormone production. Conversely, in secondary forms, an appropriate or inappropriate overproduction of EPO drives the marrow hyperplasia. This can be driven by systemic hypoxia from chronic pulmonary disorders, high-altitude adaptation, or local renal hypoxia due to renal artery stenosis, as well as EPO-secreting tumors. As red cell mass accumulates, vascular resistance rises exponentially, straining the right and left ventricles and predisposing the patient to widespread microcirculatory stasis, thrombosis, and tissue ischemia. Nurses must grasp these cellular and systemic mechanisms to comprehend why patients develop specific symptoms like plethora, headaches, and thromboembolic events, and to understand the rationale behind targeted therapies such as phlebotomy and cytoreductive agents.

headings.title: Classification: Primary versus Secondary Polycythaemia
headings.content: Polycythaemia is broadly classified into two main categories: primary and secondary polycythaemia. Primary polycythaemia, most notably exemplified by polycythaemia vera (PV), is an intrinsic clonal disorder of the bone marrow stem cells. In PV, the bone marrow produces excessive red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets independently of normal physiological stimuli. This form is frequently associated with acquired genetic mutations, such as the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene mutation. Laboratory evaluation of primary polycythaemia typically reveals a low serum erythropoietin level alongside panmyelosis. Secondary polycythaemia, on the other hand, is an extrinsic response characterized by an elevated red blood cell mass driven by increased levels of erythropoietin. This can be classified further into appropriate secondary polycythaemia, which occurs as a physiological compensation for chronic hypoxaemia—such as that seen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), cyanotic heart disease, or prolonged residence at high altitudes—and inappropriate secondary polycythaemia, where EPO is secreted autonomously by tumors like renal cell carcinoma or hepatic neoplasms in the absence of generalized hypoxia. Differentiating between primary and secondary polycythaemia is crucial for nursing and medical staff because the therapeutic goals differ significantly; primary forms often require cytoreductive therapy and serial phlebotomies, whereas secondary forms focus heavily on treating the underlying hypoxaemic or neoplastic trigger. Understanding this classification guides accurate nursing assessments, diagnostic workups, and targeted patient education.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: The etiology and risk factors for polycythaemia vary widely depending on whether the condition is primary or secondary. Primary polycythaemia vera is an acquired myeloproliferative neoplasm, meaning it develops over time due to somatic mutations rather than being inherited directly from parents. It predominantly affects older adults, with the median age of diagnosis typically between 60 and 70 years, and shows a slight male predominance. Environmental risk factors for secondary polycythaemia include chronic exposure to tobacco smoke, which introduces carbon monoxide that binds hemoglobin and reduces effective oxygen delivery, thereby stimulating compensatory erythropoiesis. Other significant risk factors involve chronic hypoxaemic disorders such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), obstructive sleep apnea, and living at high altitudes where atmospheric oxygen tension is diminished. Furthermore, pathological conditions that cause localized renal hypoxia—such as renal artery stenosis, polycystic kidney disease, or hydronephrosis—can prompt the kidneys to continuously release excessive erythropoietin. Certain renal and hepatic tumors, including renal cell carcinomas, hepatocellular carcinomas, and cerebellar hemangioblastomas, are known to ectopically secrete erythropoietin, serving as direct oncological causes of inappropriate secondary polycythaemia. Relative polycythaemia, a separate entity caused by acute plasma volume loss rather than an absolute increase in red cell mass, is often linked to risk factors like severe dehydration, extensive burns, diuretic overuse, or chronic stress-related plasma contraction known as Gaisbock syndrome. Identifying these diverse etiologies enables nurses to perform comprehensive patient histories and recognize high-risk clinical profiles.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment Findings
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of polycythaemia stem directly from hyperviscosity, expanded total blood volume, and sluggish microvascular circulation. Patients frequently present with a plethoric or ruddy complexion, characterized by a reddish-blue discoloration of the face, hands, and mucous membranes due to cutaneous vessel engorgement and slowed blood flow. Neurological symptoms are exceptionally common and include throbbing headaches, dizziness, vertigo, tinnitus, visual disturbances such as blurred vision or scotomas, and generalized fatigue resulting from impaired cerebral microcirculation. Cardiovascular manifestations may feature hypertension caused by increased systemic vascular resistance and hypervolemia, alongside angina pectoris if coronary blood flow is compromised by the thickened blood. A hallmark symptom of polycythaemia vera, in particular, is aquagenic pruritus—an intense, stinging, or itching sensation triggered by contact with water, regardless of its temperature, which is believed to be caused by mast cell degranulation and the release of histamine. Patients may also experience splenomegaly due to extramedullary haematopoiesis and the sequestration of excess blood cells, leading to early satiety or left upper quadrant abdominal fullness. Thrombotic complications can manifest as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or transient ischemic attacks, while paradoxical bleeding tendencies like easy bruising, epistaxis, or gastrointestinal bleeding can occur due to acquired platelet function defects or abnormal von Willebrand factor interactions. Nursing assessments must be systematic, focusing heavily on neurological checks, peripheral perfusion, skin integrity, and early detection of thromboembolic warning signs.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Investigations
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation of polycythaemia requires a structured cascade of laboratory investigations and clinical assessments to confirm elevated red cell mass and differentiate primary from secondary etiologies. The initial screening test is a complete blood count (CBC), which typically reveals significantly elevated haemoglobin and haematocrit levels, often exceeding 16.5 g/dL in women and 18.5 g/dL in men, frequently accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis in primary cases. Following confirmation of elevated haematocrit, serum erythropoietin (EPO) levels are measured; suppressed or low EPO strongly points toward primary polycythaemia vera, whereas normal or elevated EPO suggests secondary causes. For suspected primary cases, molecular testing for the JAK2V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutations is performed, as these are present in the vast majority of polycythaemia vera patients. Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy may be indicated to evaluate cellularity, architectural organization, and rule out other myeloproliferative neoplasms, typically demonstrating panmyelosis with hypercellular bone marrow. In cases where secondary polycythaemia is suspected, arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is crucial to detect underlying hypoxaemia, and imaging studies such as chest radiography, echocardiography, renal ultrasound, or abdominal CT scans are utilized to investigate chronic pulmonary disease, cyanotic heart defects, renal artery stenosis, or EPO-secreting tumors. Nurses play a vital role in preparing patients for these diagnostic procedures, ensuring proper fasting or positioning when necessary, and accurately documenting laboratory trends to assist the healthcare team in diagnosis and treatment planning.

headings.title: Medical and Nursing Management
headings.content: Medical and nursing management of polycythaemia focuses on reducing blood viscosity, normalizing haematocrit levels, preventing thrombotic and haemorrhagic events, and relieving distressing symptoms. The cornerstone of medical therapy for polycythaemia vera is therapeutic phlebotomy, a procedure where a specific volume of blood—typically 300 to 500 mL—is periodically withdrawn to maintain the patient's haematocrit below 45% in men and 42% in women. In addition to phlebotomy, low-dose aspirin is frequently prescribed to reduce the risk of microvascular and macrovascular thrombotic events, provided there are no contraindications such as active bleeding. Cytoreductive therapy, using agents such as hydroxyurea or interferon-alpha, may be initiated in high-risk patients—such as those over age 60 or with a history of thrombosis—to suppress excessive bone marrow cell production. For secondary polycythaemia, management shifts toward treating the underlying trigger, which may include oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia, smoking cessation programs, or surgical intervention for renal artery stenosis and EPO-secreting tumors. Nursing care encompasses rigorous monitoring of vital signs, fluid balance, and neurological status, alongside patient education on hydration to prevent worsening blood viscosity. Nurses must also monitor for complications during and after phlebotomy procedures, such as hypotension, dizziness, or vasovagal reactions, and provide emotional support as patients adjust to a chronic, lifelong condition.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Prognosis
headings.content: Potential complications of polycythaemia are largely driven by chronic hyperviscosity, abnormal platelet function, and the progressive nature of myeloproliferative disorders. The most life-threatening complications are thrombotic events, which include deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and cerebrovascular accidents. Conversely, despite the high concentration of blood cells, patients can experience severe haemorrhagic complications due to acquired von Willebrand syndrome or dysfunctional platelets, manifesting as major gastrointestinal bleeding or epistaxis. Over time, a subset of patients with primary polycythaemia vera may experience disease progression, transitioning into myelofibrosis, characterized by extensive bone marrow fibrosis, severe anaemia, and massive splenomegaly. Furthermore, there is a recognized risk of transformation into acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndrome, particularly in patients treated with certain cytoreductive agents. The overall prognosis for polycythaemia varies significantly; with prompt diagnosis, diligent therapeutic phlebotomy, and appropriate medical management, patients can live for decades with a near-normal quality of life. However, unmanaged hyperviscosity and uncontrolled thrombosis drastically reduce life expectancy. Nurses hold a pivotal role in long-term surveillance, educating patients on recognizing early signs of stroke, bleeding, or worsening fatigue, and encouraging strict adherence to follow-up schedules to optimize prognostic outcomes.
